settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: DeserializationUtils is a utility that converts the loaded object to JsonNode/expectedType via Json.mapper().convertValue; no evidence in the read spans shows the range of instantiable classes or a concrete working gadget.

The task instructions note that an index match or usage site does not prove reachability or exploitability; the exact SnakeYAML version (defined through swagger-core, not in the read pom.xml) was not confirmed, and modern SnakeYAML/Yaml defaults are safe.
candidates.description: DeserializationUtils.readYamlTree(String) and readYamlValue(String, Class) construct a plain `new org.yaml.snakeyaml.Yaml()` and call `yaml.load(contents)` on YAML content before converting it to Jackson types. For SnakeYAML versions before the hardened default (2.x), the no-argument Yaml() constructor uses the standard Constructor, which honors global tags such as `!!fully.qualified.ClassName` and can instantiate arbitrary classes with single-argument constructors or Setters present on the classpath. The YAML content here is attacker-influenceable: Swagger20Parser.convertToSwagger and Swagger20Parser.readWithInfo route non-JSON content (data that does not start with '{') from a remote URL, local file, or classpath resource to DeserializationUtils.readYamlTree, and SwaggerParser.readWithInfo(String) also calls readYamlTree on a raw string. This makes arbitrary-object-instantiation via `!!` tags a candidate in the YAML parsing path of an untrusted specification. The actual severity depends on the SnakeYAML version resolved transitively (via swagger-core) which is not defined in the read pom.
missing_evidence: The resolved SnakeYAML version and whether `new Yaml()` in that version permits arbitrary class instantiation (root pom.xml / dependencyManagement could not be read).
Proof that a YAML-tagged payload survives parsing and yields code/data impact rather than a parse failure.
Any deserialization filter, SafeConstructor usage, or class allowlist elsewhere in the codebase.
preconditions: A caller parses a spec whose content is not detected as JSON (does not start with '{') and is deserialized through DeserializationUtils.readYamlTree / readYamlValue.
The resolved SnakeYAML version still uses the permissive default constructor semantics (pre-2.0 style) for `new Yaml()`.
A suitable gadget class with a usable single-argument constructor or setter is present on the application classpath.
candidates.title: YAML parsing of untrusted spec content uses SnakeYAML default (non-safe) constructor

counter_evidence: This behavior is gated on an explicitly-set system property; the README documents it as an intentional user opt-in (TRUST_ALL=true) for self-signed/firewalled environments, so it is a documented configuration rather than an unconditional weakness.
By default (property unset/false) the returned ConnectionConfigurator is a no-op and the default JVM TLS validation applies.
candidates.description: RemoteUrl.createConnectionConfigurator() reads the system property `io.swagger.parser.util.RemoteUrl.trustAll` and, when it parses to true, installs a TrustManager that accepts every certificate (empty checkClientTrusted/checkServerTrusted, getAcceptedIssuers returns null) plus a HostnameVerifier that always returns true, wiring them into every HttpsURLConnection processed by urlToString. Because CONNECTION_CONFIGURATOR is a static final initialized once, this permissive configuration then applies to all subsequent remote spec/ref fetches in the process. RemoteUrl.urlToString is reached from Swagger20Parser.read/readWithInfo for any location starting with "http", and from RefUtils.readExternalUrlRef/readExternalRef for URL refs, i.e. for specs and external refs that may be attacker-supplied. This disables both certificate-chain validation and hostname checking, enabling machine-in-the-middle interception/modification of fetched specifications.
missing_evidence: Whether the property name expected by the code (io.swagger.parser.util.RemoteUrl.trustAll) is what deployments actually set; README references TRUST_ALL, which does not match the property key read in code, so I could not confirm a documented propagation path.
No evidence of remote/attacker control over the system property (system properties are normally operator-controlled), so this is not shown to be directly attacker-triggerable.
preconditions: The JVM is started with -Dio.swagger.parser.util.RemoteUrl.trustAll=true (or otherwise the system property is set)
The parser reads a spec or external ref over HTTPS, so the all-trusting SSLSocketFactory and hostname verifier are applied.
candidates.title: TLS certificate and hostname verification can be globally disabled for all parser HTTP connections via system property

counter_evidence: The path passed to resolve is not shown to be URL-decoded or otherwise attacker-sanitized in the read spans; normalize() only removes '..' segments textually and does not itself enforce containment, but no explicit taint from an untrusted remote document to `file` was traced end-to-end within the read spans.

Contents still have to be deserializable into the expected type (e.g. a Model) for later stages, which limits direct exfiltration; the immediate effect observable in code is reading the file, and failures raise a RuntimeException rather than echoing the content.
candidates.description: RefUtils.readExternalRef computes the target of a relative ref as `parentDirectory.resolve(file).normalize()` and then reads it with IOUtils.toString(new FileInputStream(...)) if it exists. The `file` value comes from the ref string parsed in ResolverCache.loadRef (the segment before '#/'), which originates from the (potentially untrusted, possibly remotely-fetched) specification. There is no check that the normalized path remains within parentDirectory, so a ref such as `../../../../etc/something` normalizes to a path outside the intended directory tree and causes the parser to read that file's contents. ResolverCache.loadRef invokes this path when parentDirectory is non-null (a local file parent), independently of whether the root spec itself was loaded from a remote location, so a remote spec can drive a local file read.
missing_evidence: The writer-side path where a remote spec's ref string becomes the `file` argument (paths through Deserializer/processors were not in the read spans).
Whether any earlier validation rejects '..' segments in refs.
Whether any read result is surfaced to an attacker-controlled sink (e.g. error messages, returned object) to constitute disclosure.
preconditions: A spec containing an external relative $ref (or an external $ref whose ref string contains '..' path segments) is parsed.
The parent location is a filesystem path, so ResolverCache uses parentDirectory and RefUtils.readExternalRef's non-URL branch.
The target file exists and its contents can be interpreted (or at least read) by the parser path in use.
candidates.title: Relative external $ref resolved with Path.resolve().normalize() without containment check, allowing directory traversal outside the parent directory

counter_evidence: ClassLoader#getResourceAsStream semantics restrict the lookup to classpath resources and reject some path forms; it does not grant arbitrary filesystem access and only reads resources already packaged/available on the classpath.
The returned contents are consumed as spec data and thrown into the parser rather than streamed back to a caller, so disclosure depends on further handling not visible in the read spans.
candidates.description: ClasspathHelper.loadFileFromClasspath(String location) passes the caller-provided string directly to ClasspathHelper.class.getResourceAsStream(location), then to the class loader getResourceAsStream and ClassLoader.getSystemResourceAsStream, returning the stream contents as a string. The location argument ultimately derives from the spec location or from external ref strings handled by RefUtils.readExternalRef (the fallback when the resolved file does not exist) and Swagger20Parser (fallback when a local path does not exist). This makes arbitrary classpath-resource reads a candidate: a spec or location value can select any resource visible to the application class loader (for example other configuration/DTO resources bundled on the classpath), because no normalization or allowlist is applied to the name before the lookup.
missing_evidence: Whether the resulting content (or parse errors containing it) is returned to an attacker-controlled sink.
Whether any upstream validation constrains the location/ref strings before reaching this helper.
preconditions: The parser is invoked with a location (or a relative external ref) whose value is not an existing filesystem path, so the classpath fallback is taken.
The attacker can influence that location/ref string.
A target resource exists on the classpath whose name matches the supplied string.
candidates.title: Classpath resource lookup with caller/ref-controlled path string in ClasspathHelper.loadFileFromClasspath

counter_evidence: Fetching external references is the core intended feature of the resolver (README describes reading specs from arbitrary http/file locations), so this is by-design behavior rather than a defect; no origin allowlist is present, but none is claimed either.
No evidence in the read spans shows the fetched response being returned to an attacker-controlled sink; the effect is the outbound request itself.
candidates.description: ResolverCache.loadRef splits the ref on '#/', takes the pre-fragment part as `file`, and for non-internal formats fetches it: when parentDirectory is null but rootPath is set (e.g. the root spec was loaded from a URL) it calls RefUtils.readExternalUrlRef(file, ...), and RefUtils passes URL-format refs straight to RemoteUrl.urlToString(file, auths). Nothing in the read spans restricts `file` to the same origin as the root document, so a ref string carrying an absolute http/https URL causes the parser to issue an outbound request to that URL, and relative refs are resolved against the root path by RefUtils.buildUrl. This is the classic external-reference fetch behavior that can be abused as a server-side request forgery channel when a service parses untrusted specifications.
missing_evidence: Confirmation of which call sites (processors not in the read spans) invoke loadRef with refs taken from untrusted document content at runtime.
Whether the deployment offers any network egress restrictions or allowlist outside this code.
preconditions: A service parses a spec whose $ref strings point to absolute URLs (or relative refs that resolve to attacker-chosen hosts) and resolve=true / resolution is performed.
The parsing process has network egress and the target is reachable.
candidates.title: External refs can specify absolute/remote URLs fetched by the resolver (SSRF-shaped fetch channel)
